newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - Japanese seek to shed child porn tag.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Japanese seek to shed child porn tag.

text.p: On the front cover of a Japanese magazine named "Candy Hot", a child-like Asian girl smiles wanly above a headline reading "Beauty knows no borders".
On the back cover, a series of nude photographs show her thin, hairless body in awkward poses.
The magazine is on sale in a shop in central Tokyo's Kanda district, about two km (one mile) north of the stately Imperial Palace.
Kanda is an innocuous mix of office and residential buildings which shows little evidence of the thriving pornography industry which exists there.
Respectable-looking book emporiums cluster together near Kanda's underground train station. Alongside them are shops specialising in pornography.

Many of these shops have a so-called "Children's Corner", a separate section for child pornography where topless or naked pre-pubescent girls bedeck the front and back covers of books, magazines and videos sealed in plastic bags.
SHAMING CONSUMERS
Outraged by the display, politicians and anti-pornography campaigners have banded together to try to end Japan's reputation as a haven for pornography.
Last December, the government launched a campaign to get public opinion on its side.
The campaign, advertised by posters in city centres, highlights the abuse of children by the porn industry and attempts to shame its consumers.
In the next stage, three female politicians plan to submit a bill to parliament in the next few months for a new law that would outlaw the sexual exploitation of children.
"To stop the porn we need a law against the exploitation of and cruelty to children," Lower House member Sumiko Shimizu told a recent news conference.
Shimizu, a Social Democratic Party lawmaker, said it was important to change Japanese society's view of what was and was not acceptable in the sex industry.

"The popularity of telephone clubs, where schoolgirls contact customers for sex, and the high incidence of schoolgirl prostitution in Japan are a big social problem... which goes hand in hand with the issue of the sexual exploitation of children," she said.
For weeks, Japanese media have zeroed in on so-called telephone clubs in which teenage girls aged around 13 to 15 years have told of meeting mainly middle-aged men.
The teenagers have sex with the clients so they can buy brand-name clothes and accessories in consumer-conscious Japan.

The reports have said that one of the most disturbing features of the teenage prostitution phenomenon is the premium younger girls fetch from "lolicom" clients -- older men with "Lolita complexes" for little girls.
NO LAWS AGAINST CHILD PORN
"There is absolutely no legislation against this kind of (Lolicom) pornography here...not against the production, sale or possession of it," says anti-child prostitution activist Shiro Yoshioka.
"And yet there are 46 countries which forbid the sale of child pornography and 36 which ban the possession of it," he said.

The United Nations children's organisation UNICEF said in an annual report last December that at least one million girls and an uncertain number of boys were exploited by the sex industry throughout the world.
UNICEF's Japan representative, Akihiro Hagio, says the number of children used by the Asian sex trade runs into the hundreds of thousands, topped by Thailand's notorious sex trade.
"Thai police estimate the number of children in the sex trade at 160,000, but non-governmental organisations say the figure is more like 400,000 children," Hagio said.
Recent years have seen Japanese nationals on trial in child sex cases in Thailand and the Philippines, crystallising an image of large numbers of Japanese visitors seeking sex with children.
"Japanese tourists have a very bad name... Anyone who goes to Southeast Asia can see that," Hagio told Reuters.

Activist Yoshioka says the government campaign faces an uphill battle because of widespread indifference in Japanese society to child sexual exploitation overseas and a tolerance of the image of children as sex objects.
"At last the Japanese government is taking action...it's about public awareness and changing the law. That's our work from now on," he said.
